title: Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange
short: Two people agree on a secret g^(ab) mod p while sharing only gᵃ and gᵇ in public.
trouble: Students compute the shared key as gᵃ · gᵇ = g^(a + b) instead of (gᵃ)ᵇ = g^(ab).

blocks.html: Every cipher so far needs a shared secret key. But how do two people who have never met agree on a key, over a line that anyone can listen to? In 1976 Diffie and Hellman found a way, built on discrete logarithms: easy to go forward, hard to go back.

items: Public: a large prime $p$ and a primitive root $g$ mod $p$.
Alice picks a secret $a$ and sends $A = g^{a} \bmod p$. Bob picks a secret $b$ and sends $B = g^{b} \bmod p$.
Alice computes $B^{a}$, Bob computes $A^{b}$. Both get the shared key $K = g^{ab} \bmod p$.

blocks.html: $B^{a} = (g^{b})^{a} = g^{ab} = (g^{a})^{b} = A^{b}$, so they agree. An eavesdropper, Eve, sees $p$, $g$, $A$ and $B$. To get $K$ she seems to need $a$ or $b$, that is, a discrete logarithm of $A$ or $B$. For a prime of a few hundred digits, no one knows how to do that in any reasonable time, while Alice and Bob each need only one fast power.

blocks.title: A small exchange
blocks.q: Public: $p = 29$, $g = 2$. Alice's secret is $a = 9$ and Bob's is $b = 13$. Find $A$, $B$ and the shared key.

blocks.title: Eve with a tiny prime
steps: Eve lists $2^{1}, 2^{2}, \dots \bmod 29$ until she sees $19$: $2^{9} \equiv 19$, so $a = 9$.
Then she computes $B^{a} = 14^{9} \equiv 3$, the key. With $p$ near $10^{600}$ the list would be far too long to search.
blocks.a: A small prime makes the discrete logarithm easy.

blocks.html: Computing the shared key as $A \cdot B$. That is $g^{a} g^{b} = g^{a + b}$, not $g^{ab}$, and it is no secret at all: Eve sees $A$ and $B$ and can multiply them. Here $A \cdot B = 19 \cdot 14 = 266 \equiv 5$, not the key $3$. The key comes from raising the other person's number to your own secret exponent.

Why a primitive root? Then $g^{a}$ runs through every nonzero residue as $a$ varies, so the shared key can be any of $p - 1$ values and Eve gains nothing from guessing. If $g$ had a small order, say 4, there would be only 4 possible keys.

Diffie–Hellman protects against listening, not against impersonation: an attacker who can change messages could run one exchange with Alice and another with Bob. Real systems add signatures to prove who is talking.
Diffie–Hellman: exchange $A = g^{a}$ and $B = g^{b}$ in public; each side raises the other's number to its own secret, and both get $g^{ab} \bmod p$.
